newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia says Singapore ties need time to heal.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia says Singapore ties need time to heal.

text.p: The Malaysian government on Wednesday accepted an apology by Singapore Senior Minister Lee Kuan Yew for disparaging remarks about a Malaysian state, but said the damage done would take time to heal.

Foreign Minister Abdullah Badawi told reporters the government accepted Lee's apology for describing the south Malaysian state of Johore as "notorious for shootings, muggings and car-jackings" in a Singapore court affidavit.
Abdullah said after a cabinet meeting that Malaysia also viewed positively Lee's move to have the offending remarks deleted from the affidavit.
"The Malaysian government accepts the unreserved apology tendered by Senior Minister Lee Kuan Yew and views positively his intention to retract the offending paragraphs," he said.

"However, it should be acknowledged that this episode has deeply hurt Malaysians of all sections of society and that restoration of the old level of relationship would take time," he said in a two-paragraph statement.
Abdullah declined to elaborate or answer questions.

The statement appeared to defuse one of the worst diplomatic rows in years between two countries who were once united as British colonies but who are competing fiercely for regional economic power and influence.
At the height of the row last week, Malaysians in Johor, just across the Johor Strait from Singapore, brandished placards calling Lee "stupid", "senile" and a "bloody idiot".

Lee's comments on Johor became front-page news in the Malaysian media after the affidavit he filed on January 27 as part of a libel suit against Singapore opposition politician Tang Liang Hong was leaked to the media.

Tang, who had criticised the ruling People's Action Party in Singapore during campaigning for general elections this year, fled to Johor Baru, the capital of Johor state, after losing a race for a parliament seat in the January 2 elections. He later said he left Singapore because he feared for his life.
Lee, however, questioned Tang's decision for choosing Johor, saying "that place is notorious for shootings, muggings and car-jackings".

Following the furore caused in Malaysia by his statement, the 73-year-old elder statesman, who led the fight for Singapore's independence and was its prime minister from 1959 until 1990, issued a statement through his office apologising "unreservedly" for his remarks on Johor.
But Malaysians remained enraged, demanding he retract the remarks in the court affidavit. The youth wing of Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad's party even threatened to sue Lee.
Mahathir, refusing to let his neighbour off the hook, said during the week: "We in the government have always had problems with Singapore."
Finally, in a signed statement on Tuesday, Lee repeated his apology and said he had instructed his lawyer to ask the court's permission to have the remarks on Johor deleted.
Born from the same British imperial legacy and united briefly from 1963 to 1965, Malaysia and Singapore have close-knit economic, political and cultural ties -- and a history of spats.

Singapore imports much of its food, water and raw materials from across the Johor Strait and is among the biggest investors in Malaysia. Tens of thousands of Malaysians fill jobs in the island-state's labour-short economy.
